pages.title: Repository Overview: composio
pages.content:
## Project Summary

Composio is an end-to-end developer toolkit platform for AI agents: it consumes your per-user session context and requested app capabilities, runs a tool/connection execution pipeline (including authentication and metadata discovery when needed), and outputs an agent-ready “tools surface” plus executed actions across 1000+ apps. You use it by creating a session, handing the session’s tools to your agent, and letting Composio turn intent into action via a consistent SDK and provider layer; outputs include session-scoped tool execution, connected-account linking, and toolkit/tool-router behavior suitable for multi-turn agent flows.

Composio combines distinct evidence/intelligence views so the agent experience stays both correct and usable: (1) a session-centric execution model that decides how to execute tools at runtime, (2) SDK-layer abstractions that expose a stable interface across languages, and (3) a documentation/knowledge layer that stays fresh by verifying published catalog claims against production snapshots during data refresh. The execution views focus on “what happens when a tool is invoked,” while the docs/KB views focus on “what the agent should reliably know and how to use it”—with guardrails ensuring generated code follows Composio patterns.

## Architecture

At the center is the session-based execution engine: `ts/packages/core/src/composio.ts` is the main SDK entry that constructs configured clients and orchestrates calls into core models; `ts/packages/core/src/models/SessionContext.ts` is where execution logic is applied to a specific user/session context, ensuring the right auth/tooling strategy is selected per turn. The engine delegates actual routing to `ts/packages/core/src/models/ToolRouterSession.ts`, which executes the tool router flow (including meta-tool behaviors) so “tool execution” doesn’t require you to preload hundreds of tool definitions or auth configuration into your agent context.

The provider layer adapts those core concepts to an agent framework’s native tool format. For example, `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/index.ts` implements TypesafeProvider::execute, converting Composio’s execution results into the provider’s expected output shape for your agent integration. This separation lets the SDK keep a consistent execution contract while providers specialize the “bridge to the editor” and framework integration.

The CLI is a first-class operational surface for local workflows. `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/core/entry.ts` is the CLI’s operational entry point for key handling, while the broader CLI package owns command UX and tests as a convenience layer for developers (including local tool surface flows for coding agents). This is distinct from the SDK runtime path: the CLI is how you initiate and manage interactions from a shell, whereas the SDK is how you embed Composio in application code.

The documentation/knowledge layer is maintained alongside the runtime system. `docs` owns the docs site and content workflows, while the repo’s knowledge base freshness verification decision ensures published guides are mechanically checked against refreshed production snapshots instead of relying only on calendar-based review. In practice, the docs lifecycle has its own “maintenance path” (refresh + verify) and “use path” (serve verified toolkit/guide content to onboarding/RAG), which complements the runtime “execute path” without conflating them.

A shared index connects what the system knows about toolkits to what it displays and how it validates claims. The “maintenance” work updates stored evidence during refresh jobs, and a subsequent verification step checks mechanical claims against the same snapshot the docs site is about to ship; the “use” work queries and presents toolkit and guidance content in the docs/KB surface while the runtime session engine executes the corresponding tool/router behaviors when an agent actually performs an action.

Finally, cycles in the architecture are intentional: the session engine needs toolkit/tool-router facts to execute, while the docs/KB needs catalog facts to remain authoritative; both use the same conceptual “toolkit snapshot” idea, but each owns its lifecycle (runtime correctness vs. published knowledge correctness). The weight sits in the core execution path (ts/packages/core/...) and the docs evidence lifecycle (`docs`), because those are the two surfaces that must stay correct under change.

## Key concepts

- **Session**
  A per-user, per-conversation execution context that you create and reuse; it scopes authentication, tool availability, and runtime execution behavior so agents don’t have to be configured with every possible toolkit in each turn.

- **Tool Router session API**
  A session-scoped routing layer that drives tool execution (including meta behaviors) so the system can select the right execution strategy for connected accounts and toolkits at runtime, rather than relying on static preloading.

- **Meta tools**
  Built-in runtime “discover/auth/execute” behaviors that reduce context bloat: instead of loading a large list of tool definitions, the session can discover and prepare the needed tool surface as the agent asks for actions.

- **Provider**
  An adapter that translates Composio execution results into your agent framework’s native tool shape; providers implement the integration “bridge” while keeping the underlying execution contract consistent.

- **Toolkit snapshots**
  Generated, authoritative toolkit evidence used by the docs/KB surface; toolkit pages can fall back to production querying when a slug is absent, but the intended model is snapshot-first to keep catalog and knowledge verification deterministic.

- **LLM guardrails**
  Invisible, per-page frontmatter-scoped instructions injected into docs responses so code generators use the correct Composio SDK patterns; this turns documentation into safer, more predictable agent output.

- **KB freshness verification**
  A mechanical verification step that checks published knowledge against refreshed production snapshots during the docs data refresh lifecycle, reducing drift between what guides claim and what the system actually supports.

## Generated package surface (the persistence boundary for types)

The “persistence boundary” for this subsystem is the generated artifact set under `ts/packages/core/pack/generated/`, which forms the stable TypeScript-facing entrypoint outputs consumed by downstream code. The group includes both the compiled JavaScript entry (`index.js`) and the type declarations (`index.d.ts`), plus the package-generated index that represents the consolidated surface.

| Artifact role | Path |
|---|---|
| Type declarations entrypoint | `ts/packages/core/pack/generated/index.d.ts` |
| JavaScript entrypoint | `ts/packages/core/pack/generated/index.js` |
| Generated index surface (package entry) | `ts/packages/core/pack/generated/index.d.ts`, `ts/packages/core/pack/generated/index.js` |

Because these are generated outputs, the rest of the subsystem’s job is to ensure the inputs (configuration + generation scripts + type tests) keep producing consistent artifacts.

## Type/doc generation pipeline (build-time orchestration)

The core orchestration for generation lives in `ts/packages/core/scripts/generate-docs.ts`, which is also the subsystem’s most active file in recent history (7 commits in 90 days). This script is the focal point for producing documentation/type-related outputs that get checked by the repo’s test harness.

This subsystem’s intent is clear from its neighbors: `ts/packages/core/test/scripts/generate-docs.test.ts` depends on the generation script as a correctness gate, meaning generation is treated as a first-class, testable build step rather than a developer-only convenience.

### Inputs and outputs (as evidenced by the file set)

While the internal implementation details aren’t described in this material, the repository signals show a consistent pattern:

- It integrates with external tooling used for type/doc workflows (notably `tsdown`, and `@arethetypeswrong/cli` as part of type-quality automation).
- It produces generated artifacts under `ts/packages/core/pack/generated/` (since both the JS and `d.ts` entrypoints exist under that path).
- It is verified via `ts/packages/core/test/scripts/generate-docs.test.ts` (dependency relation listed for this page’s scope).

## Build configuration and bundling behavior (tsdown integration)

This package also owns its build-time bundling configuration via `ts/packages/core/tsdown.config.ts`, which appears as the most co-changed, bug-fix-heavy file in recent history (“most in `ts/packages/core/tsdown.config.ts`”). That history aligns with the subsystem’s core responsibility: ensuring the generated artifact surface stays correct and up to date when bundling and type packaging rules change.

A base configuration is pulled in from `tsdown.config.base.ts`, showing that the core package specializes a shared tsdown baseline rather than inventing its own bundling semantics.

### Configuration relationships

| Relationship type | Path |
|---|---|
| Consumes shared tsdown base config | `tsdown.config.base.ts` |
| Owns tsdown package config | `ts/packages/core/tsdown.config.ts` |

## Type-level verification (d.ts tests as a contract)

A defining concern of this subsystem is enforcing correctness of the public type surface using type tests. The repository includes a cluster of `ts/packages/core/type-tests/*.test-d.ts` files focused on contract-level behaviors—especially around JSON schema properties and configuration mapping.

These tests function as the contract that protects the generated `index.d.ts` surface from accidental drift, especially when the generator and tsdown config evolve.

| Test focus | Test file |
|---|---|
| JSON schema property typings | `ts/packages/core/type-tests/json-schema-property.test-d.ts` |
| Session/config typing surface | `ts/packages/core/type-tests/session-configs.test-d.ts` |
| Sessions—MCP related typings | `ts/packages/core/type-tests/sessions-mcp.test-d.ts` |
| Toolkit auth field mapping typing | `ts/packages/core/type-tests/toolkit-auth-field-mapping.test-d.ts` |

In combination with the generated artifacts boundary (`ts/packages/core/pack/generated/index.d.ts`), these type tests ensure the subsystem produces stable, verifiable outputs without needing runtime execution to validate correctness.

## Test execution integration (vitest configuration)

The subsystem also includes test orchestration via `ts/packages/core/vitest.config.ts`, ensuring that the generation checks and type tests run in the repo’s expected testing environment. This is part of why the type/doc generation script is not “fire-and-forget”: the package owns the local test wiring needed to keep the build-time pipeline reliable.

## External tooling the package relies on (automation surface)

This subsystem’s correctness depends on multiple external tools that are clearly represented in the listed dependencies. The following are the notable ones relevant to the scaffold/generation/type-quality workflow:

| Tool | Listed as external system used |
|---|---|
| Type-testing / lint-like checks | `@arethetypeswrong/cli` |
| Release/versioning automation | `@changesets/cli`, `@changesets/read` |
| Test environment types | `@types/bun`, `@types/node`, `@types/semver` |
| Test UI | `@vitest/ui` |
| Git hooks | `husky`, `lint-staged` |
| Lint/format ecosystem | `oxlint`, `oxlint-plugin-eslint`, `prettier` |
| Package validation | `publint`, `semver`, `tsdown` |

These tools collectively support the “generated artifacts and correctness gates” responsibility captured by the presence of `tsdown` config, doc generation script, and `.test-d.ts` contract checks.

## Health and coupling signals (what tends to change together)

The subsystem shows two important operational characteristics from git history:

- **Single-maintainer risk:** 4 files have a bus factor of one (single-maintainer risk), and **`ts/packages/core/scripts/generate-docs.ts`** is the most active file.
- **Hotspot for change:** 1 file is flagged as a change hotspot, and **`ts/packages/core/tsdown.config.ts`** has the bulk of recent bug-fix commits.

Additionally, there is hidden change coupling that isn’t explained by import graphs: `ts/packages/core` co-changes with `docs`, `python`, `ts/packages/cli-keyring`, and `ts/packages/cli`. That implies the generated/type artifacts and their documentation workflow are downstream dependencies for release and cross-language or cross-package integration, even though runtime session/provider behavior is explicitly out of scope for this subsystem’s page.

Potentially unused private symbols are present (e.g., `SCRIPT_DIR`, `PACKAGE_DIR`, `MODELS_DIR`, `OUTPUT_DIR`, `TEMP_JSON`, `TYPEDOC_BIN`, `INTERNAL_CLASSES`, `USER_INSTANTIATED_CLASSES`, `DISPLAY_NAME_OVERRIDES`, `SLUG_OVERRIDES`), suggesting portions of the generation scaffolding may have been partially refactored or left behind by earlier iterations—another reason this package emphasizes tests and generated artifacts as guardrails.

pages.title: Core Overview
pages.content:
## What this subsystem is responsible for (and what it doesn’t)

Within `ts/packages/core/src`, the “core” responsibility is to provide consistent types and semantics across the system: it concentrates (1) error classes grounded in a shared `ComposioError` hierarchy, (2) the provider base abstractions (`BaseProvider` and its agentic/non-agentic specializations), (3) the core typed definitions used to validate/describe auth and tool-related configuration, and (4) utilities that support cross-cutting concerns like logging and environment constants. The child pages are where those concerns are documented in detail; this overview focuses on how the sets fit together and what the subsystem exposes to callers.

What it deliberately leaves to other pages:
- Concrete provider runtime behavior and composition—documented under `ts/packages/core/src/lib`.
- Domain modeling for connections/tools—documented under `ts/packages/core/src/models`.
- API/shape types—documented under `ts/packages/core/src/types`.
- General utilities (including logging/env/constants)—documented under `ts/packages/core/src/utils`.

## How the parts fit together

At a high level, this subsystem wires together three layers that show up across the file set:

1. **Public surface + export boundary**
   - `ts/packages/core/src/index.ts` is the entry that downstream packages and examples consume, and the file is the natural place where the subsystem’s public symbols become visible to the rest of the repo.

2. **Semantics: errors and auth/tool typing**
   - `ts/packages/core/src/errors/ComposioError.ts` establishes the shared error base, and the other error classes listed below extend it to give stable, typed failure modes for connected accounts and auth configuration.
   - Typed definitions in `ts/packages/core/src/types/*` (notably tool types and auth config types) provide the contract language that providers and models agree on. This is the typed “glue” that keeps tool execution routing and auth configuration coherent across packages.

3. **Behavioral abstractions: provider base classes + runtime utilities**
   - `ts/packages/core/src/provider/BaseProvider.ts` defines the provider abstraction layer, and the class hierarchy then branches into agentic vs non-agentic providers (with `ComposioProvider` extending the non-agentic variant).
   - Runtime support utilities (e.g., logging and environment helpers) provide shared operational behavior that providers and examples can depend on consistently.

Those layers converge at the same point: downstream code imports from the core package, relies on the shared error semantics and typed contracts, and then instantiates/uses providers via the base abstractions. The e2e tests and examples across runtimes and tool routers demonstrate that this subsystem is not just type-only—it’s the runtime foundation that those integrations expect to exist.

## Key symbols and the responsibilities they imply

The following key files anchor the subsystem’s cross-cutting concerns:

| Location | What it anchors in the subsystem |
|---|---|
| `ts/packages/core/src/index.ts` | The subsystem’s export boundary and public entry for downstream imports |
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/ComposioError.ts` | The shared error base class used by connected-account/auth failures |
| `ts/packages/core/src/provider/BaseProvider.ts` | The provider abstraction layer that other provider classes build on |
| `ts/packages/core/src/types/tool.types.ts` | Tool-related typed contracts that downstream models/providers share |
| `ts/packages/core/src/types/authConfigs.types.ts` | Auth configuration typing that keeps auth config consistent system-wide |
| `ts/packages/core/src/types/connectedAccountAuthStates.types.ts` | Connected-account auth state typing |
| `ts/packages/core/src/types/modifiers.types.ts` | Modifier/behavior typing used in tool/provider interactions |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/logger.ts` | Logging helper used as a shared operational utility |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/env.ts` | Environment/config helpers used to parameterize runtime behavior |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/constants.ts` | Shared constants used across runtime paths |

## Error semantics: stable failure modes across connected accounts

The error hierarchy in this subsystem is explicitly structured to extend `ComposioError`, making connected-account and configuration failures predictable for callers:

| Error type | Inheritance | Where it fits |
|---|---|---|
| `ComposioAPIKeyKindError` | extends `ComposioError` | API key kind mismatch / validation failures |
| `ComposioAclOnlyForSharedError` | extends `ComposioError` | Access control constraint failures |
| `ComposioAuthConfigNotFoundError` | extends `ComposioError` | Missing auth configuration |
| `ComposioBlockedInternalUrlError` | extends `ComposioError` | Internal URL blocking constraints |
| `ComposioConnectedAccountNotFoundError` | extends `ComposioError` | Connected account lookup failures |

This error layer is part of the core’s “semantics contract”: downstream examples and e2e runtimes can consistently detect and react to core failures rather than parsing messages.

## Provider abstraction: base classes used by concrete providers

The subsystem’s provider model is built from a base abstraction and refined into agentic vs non-agentic variants:

- `BaseAgenticProvider` extends `BaseProvider`
- `BaseNonAgenticProvider` extends `BaseProvider`
- `ComposioProvider` extends `BaseNonAgenticProvider`

This is the structural reason the core can support different runtime styles while keeping the rest of the system anchored to shared types (tool/auth models) and shared operational utilities (logging/env/constants). The concrete implementations live elsewhere, but the abstraction contracts live here—so consumers only need to rely on the base layer and its typed inputs/outputs.

## Typed API shapes and tool/auth configuration contracts

The types under `ts/packages/core/src/types/*` are where the subsystem formalizes the shapes other layers share. The key file signals—`tool.types.ts`, `authConfigs.types.ts`, `connectedAccountAuthStates.types.ts`, and `modifiers.types.ts`—indicate that core’s typed surface covers:

- **Tool definitions** (used by models/providers/routing integrations)
- **Auth configuration** and its **connected-account auth state**
- **Modifiers** that affect how tool/provider interactions are interpreted

This typed layer is what makes the core usable by both runtime integrations and higher-level examples without each integration reinventing shape definitions.

## Operational utilities: logging, environment, constants

The utilities under `ts/packages/core/src/utils/*` provide the “small but system-wide” operational primitives that show up repeatedly across the rest of the codebase:

- `ts/packages/core/src/utils/logger.ts` for shared logging conventions
- `ts/packages/core/src/utils/env.ts` for environment/config reading helpers
- `ts/packages/core/src/utils/constants.ts` for centralized values

Because these utilities are imported widely (indirectly across providers, models, and examples), they also contribute to the subsystem’s change-hotspot profile noted in git history.

## Built-in hygiene decisions that affect the public surface

The subsystem has an explicit architectural decision to **sanitize public docstrings in connected accounts**: internal references and incorrect statements were removed from public JSDoc (including PR references and backend/storage/user-project assumptions). This hygiene decision is not just editorial—it’s part of how core manages what information is safe to expose through its public API, which in turn is crucial since this package is imported by many downstream examples and e2e runtimes.

## Dependencies: what core relies on, and why that matters

Core’s external dependency set is small but important:

| Depends on | Role in this subsystem’s ecosystem |
|---|---|
| `ts/packages/core/package.json` | Package metadata and dependency wiring for the core distribution |
| `ts/packages/json-schema-to-zod/src/index.ts` | Enables JSON-schema-to-Zod typing integration used by downstream typed flows |

This limited dependency graph helps keep core as a stable foundation for other packages rather than a heavy integration layer.

## How downstream consumers use this subsystem

The import graph shows core is directly used by multiple runtimes and examples—particularly tool-router AI/file tool-router flows and connected-accounts examples—indicating that core must provide consistent runtime semantics and not merely compile-time types:

- Cloudflare e2e runtimes (basic, files, and tool-router AI) import core from `ts/e2e-tests/.../src/index.ts`
- Node e2e tests for “tool-router zod v3/v4” import core through `ts/e2e-tests/.../e2e.test.ts`
- Examples across anthropic, connected-accounts, error-handling, file-handling, google, and langchain import core APIs

That breadth aligns with the observed history pattern: the subsystem has **19 change hotspots** and **52 bus-factor-one files**, so the core package is both widely depended on and highly sensitive to correctness in a few critical areas.

## Health and history signals that shape how readers should navigate core

Evidence from git history indicates where attention naturally concentrates:
- **Hotspot concentration**: 19 files are flagged as change hotspots, and many bug-fix commits cluster in `ts/packages/core/src/utils/jsonSchema.ts`.
- **Maintenance risk**: 52 files have a bus factor of one, meaning knowledge is concentrated.
- **Stability pockets**: 4 files are reported as stable, which likely correspond to foundational contracts rather than frequently adjusted internals.
- **Ongoing evolution**: `ts/packages/core/src/models/ToolRouterSession.ts` is the most active file recently (12 commits in 90 days), suggesting tool-router session behavior is actively refined.

These signals reinforce why this overview points readers to the child pages: the “where” matters for safe navigation because the subsystem’s change pressure is not uniform.

## Where to go next in the documentation

- `ts/packages/core/src/lib` — provider runtime internals and how the base abstractions are realized at runtime.
- `ts/packages/core/src/models` — connection and tool domain models, including session/domain shapes used by routing and connected-account flows.
- `ts/packages/core/src/types` — typed API contracts for tool/auth/configuration/modifiers and related shapes.
- `ts/packages/core/src/utils` — shared utilities (logging/env/constants and other cross-cutting helpers) that other parts rely on.

pages.content:
## What this subsystem models: auth configs, connections, and custom tool routing/session

This group of model definitions establishes the data contract used across connection flows and tool-routing flows. It covers:

- **Auth configuration for connections**, including session/config shapes and associated conflict semantics (via model definitions that are used with the session-config conflict logic imported by other modules).
- **Connected accounts and their auth states**, including usage/account lifecycle concerns and error surfaces when states are invalid.
- **Connection requests**, i.e., the structured representation of “a caller wants to connect something,” together with the domain errors used to reject/validate invalid requests.
- **Custom tools and toolkits**, including how tools are defined and grouped, and how tool routing relates to session context (including MCP-related models).
- **Tool router session support**, such as session-specific tool/router artifacts and file mounts models (as referenced by the model/type imports used by routing/session tooling).

The subsystem’s shape is reinforced by the fact that it is heavily exercised by model-level tests (e.g., `customTool*`, `customToolkits*`, `keyring`, `logs`, `mcp`, `sessionConfigs`, `toolRouter`, `toolkitScopes`, `toolkits`, and triggers/webhooks verification), and by recent history clustering in `ts/packages/core/src/models/ToolRouterSession.ts`.

## Key model files and their roles

| File | Primary concern in the Connection and Tool Models subsystem |
|---|---|
| `ts/packages/core/src/models/CustomTool.ts` | The canonical model for representing a custom tool definition that downstream routing/session logic can interpret. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/models/CustomToolkits.ts` | The model layer for grouping/packaging tools into toolkits and expressing toolkit-level structure. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/models/ToolRouterSession.ts` | Session-scoped routing/session artifacts for tool execution planning; this is the most change-active file in the subsystem’s recent history. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/models/SessionConfigs.ts` | Auth/session configuration models that are used in conjunction with session configuration conflict logic elsewhere. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/models/Experimental.ts` | Experimental model definitions that are still part of the same contract surface as stable models (consumed by `ts/packages/core/src/experimental/index.ts`). |
| `ts/packages/core/src/models/Usage.ts` | Usage-related models that support tracking/attribution for connection/tool activity. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/models/Keyring.ts` | Model definitions for secure key material handling boundaries (as represented in model form, not execution/persistence). |
| `ts/packages/core/src/models/Webhooks.ts` | Model definitions for webhook registration/verification flows and related trigger surfaces. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/models/MCP.ts` | Models related to MCP integration, included alongside custom tool routing/session concerns. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/models/Logs.ts` | Model definitions for log records produced by connection/tool execution-related flows. |

## Domain invariants enforced via model-level error surfaces

Rather than implementing validation or transport, this subsystem is organized around *error taxonomy* imports that are paired with model definitions. The model layer is designed so that orchestration layers (and callers) can fail fast with consistent domain errors coming from:

| Error module | How it relates to these models |
|---|---|
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/AuthConfigErrors.ts` | Auth config validation outcomes for the auth/session configuration models. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/ConnectedAccountsErrors.ts` | Errors for invalid connected account states and connected-account lifecycle handling. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/ConnectionRequestErrors.ts` | Errors tied to request formation/validation around connection requests. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/ToolErrors.ts` | Tool/model-level failures relevant to custom tools and toolkits. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/ToolRouterErrors.ts` | Failures related to tool routing/session behavior modeled here. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/TriggerErrors.ts` | Errors for trigger-related flows represented by webhook/trigger models. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/ValidationErrors.ts` | General model-validation error building blocks used across model flows. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/SDKErrors.ts` | Shared SDK error surfaces used across the model boundary. |

This organization matters because the model definitions are imported by orchestration entry points such as `ts/packages/core/src/composio.ts` and by public SDK exports (`ts/packages/core/src/index.ts`), so the error types need to align with the contract that those exports expose.

## How session and tool routing concerns are represented

The subsystem’s most active area is the session-scoped routing model set—especially `ts/packages/core/src/models/ToolRouterSession.ts` (12 commits in 90 days, and the most prominent hotspot signal: 58 bug-fix commits concentrated in this file). This activity aligns with how other modules import tool-router session helpers and parameters, such as:

- `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterSessionDelete.ts`
- `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterSourceSessionConfig.ts`
- `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterParams.ts`
- `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterMcp.ts`
- `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterConstants.ts`

Even though those helpers perform routing/session operations, this subsystem defines the *models* that make those operations possible and testable (and that are exercised in `ts/packages/core/test/models/toolRouter.test.ts`, `ToolRouterSessionFilesMount.test.ts`, and the custom tool routing tests).

Relatedly, the model boundary references session-context and file-mount types indirectly through imported types such as `ts/packages/core/src/types/ToolRouterSessionFilesMount.types.ts`, ensuring the models can express “what” is mounted/available during a router session without embedding platform-specific mounting logic.

## Public documentation hygiene for connected accounts

A deliberate architectural decision shapes the connected-account models: **public docstrings in connected accounts are sanitized**. Internal references were removed from public-facing JSDoc, including examples like Hermes PR numbers and backend storage references, plus incorrect statements about users belonging to projects. The same sweep looked for similar documentation leaks in the PR diff. This is a rare “non-code” decision that still materially affects the model layer, because these docstrings ship as part of the public API surface that callers read alongside model types.

- **Hotspots:** 8 files flagged as change hotspots, consistent with the subsystem being both central and evolving.

## Contract-first type modeling for tool routing sessions

At the architectural level, `ts/packages/core/src/types` functions like the persistence boundary for “what is allowed to exist” in a tool router session and how the core runtime should interpret auth inputs. The types in this group cover:

- tool router session structures, including **tool routing parameters** and **session file mounts**
- request-level shapes, including **request options** and **connected-account context**
- authentication configuration and state for connected accounts, including **auth configs** and their **connected-account auth states**
- additional tool variants (custom tools, modifiers) and provider-facing options
- MCP configuration-related structures and schemas used by core’s MCP integration

This contract is then imported by core orchestration and model layers (for example `ts/packages/core/src/models/*` and `ts/packages/core/src/lib/*`) to ensure a consistent, strongly-typed interface between the runtime code and the caller-facing API.

## Enumerated surface: the files that define the shared shapes

The group’s public symbols and file mix show a deliberate emphasis on tool router and auth modeling—especially around the session and tool-routing interfaces.

| Area of concern | Key files (highest PageRank first) | What this signals about the subsystem |

| Tool router session and routing contracts | `ts/packages/core/src/types/tool.types.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/types/toolRouter.types.ts` | Central place where session-oriented routing shapes are defined; matches the change hotspot history concentrated in `ts/packages/core/src/types/toolRouter.types.ts`. |

| Tool variation and composition | `ts/packages/core/src/types/customTool.types.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/types/modifiers.types.ts` | Custom tooling and modifiers are modeled as types that compose into the router session contracts rather than being handled ad hoc. |
| MCP-facing shape definitions | `ts/packages/core/src/types/mcp.types.ts` | MCP integration depends on these shared type definitions to keep MCP-specific contracts consistent across core components. |

## Dependency boundary: what this type layer imports (and why it stays “pure”)

This subsystem has a small set of imports listed under “Depends on”, and those imports are narrowly aligned with constants or schema generation rather than operational logic. That’s consistent with the subsystem’s stated scope: it defines shapes without implementing effects or utilities.

## Shared-shape consumers: where these contracts flow next

The dependency list under “Depended on by” is extensive and touches both the orchestration (`ts/packages/core/src/lib/*`) and model layer (`ts/packages/core/src/models/*`). That breadth shows this subsystem is the shared contract that keeps these neighboring modules aligned.

Representative consumers include:

- `ts/packages/core/src/composio.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/index.ts`, and `ts/packages/core/src/experimental/index.ts` (public entry points that expose typed APIs)
- `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterMcp.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterParams.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterSessionDelete.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterSourceSessionConfig.ts` (session/router operations that rely on the shapes)
- `ts/packages/core/src/models/AuthConfigs.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/models/ConnectedAccounts.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/models/ConnectionRequest.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/models/CustomTool.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/models/MCP.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/models/SessionConfigs.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/models/ToolRouterSession.ts` (state and configuration models built to match these contracts)

Given the bus-factor signal (12 files with a bus factor of one), changes to these shapes are especially sensitive: they are imported widely, so even small contract edits can create broad compile-time ripple effects across core and providers.

## Architectural decisions baked into the type surface

This subsystem’s type documentation is treated as part of the contract, not merely developer-facing notes. One explicit decision reflects how the team managed the “publicness” of the connected-account API:

- **Sanitize public docstrings in connected accounts** — public docstrings/JSDoc were scrubbed to remove internal references (example signals include Hermes PR numbers, backend storage details, and incorrect statements about users belonging to projects). The change also swept for similar documentation leaks in the PR diff.

This matters because these type definitions are likely used both for compile-time safety and for API documentation generation/consumption—so the “shape + docs” together become a public interface.

## Stability and churn patterns: why tool-router types dominate evolution

pages.content:
## What this utilities subsystem actually provides

Across the 29 TypeScript utility files, the group’s responsibilities cluster into a few recurring “plumbing” roles that support the rest of `ts/packages/core`:

- **Normalization utilities** for values that need consistent formatting or interpretation (e.g., environment-derived values, constants, MIME/content handling, JSON/schema transformations).
- **Operational helpers** that control runtime behavior safely (notably cancellation).
- **Serialization / parsing helpers** that turn remote or tool-oriented payloads into predictable forms (e.g., response body reading; JSON schema to Zod usage through a dedicated integration).
- **Safety/guardrails** for file and tool-related workflows (e.g., sensitive upload paths).
- **Schema/transform logic** concentrated in the utilities layer (with `jsonSchema.ts` being the highest-activity file in recent history).

This page is intentionally scoped to what `ts/packages/core/src/utils` does; it does *not* attempt to document configuration defaulting logic (called out as excluded), which belongs in other sibling pages.

## Key files that define the subsystem’s behavior

The subsystem’s behavior is not just a collection of unrelated helpers; it’s anchored by a small set of high-leverage utilities that other modules repeatedly import.

| File | What it contributes to the utilities subsystem (behavioral role) |
|---|---|
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/logger.ts` | Centralized logging behavior used by the utilities and, indirectly, by modules that call into these utilities. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/env.ts` | Environment-related helpers—important because multiple parts of the core layer need consistent env access/derivation. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/constants.ts` | Shared constants that other utilities and downstream modules use for consistent decisions. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/jsonSchema.ts` | JSON-schema-centric transformation/resolution logic; also the most active utility file in recent history (10 commits in 90 days). |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/transform.ts` | Generic transformation helpers that utilities and higher-level logic can reuse to reshape data safely. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/cancellation.ts` | Cancellation utilities that allow higher-level operations to stop work predictably. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/readResponseBody.ts` | Response-body reading/normalization logic used when payloads come from network/tool-style operations. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/mime.ts` | MIME/content-type handling to classify payloads correctly across tool/file flows. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/toolArguments.ts` | Tool argument shaping/validation glue for downstream tool execution and routing. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/sensitiveFileUploadPaths.ts` | Guardrails around file upload paths, constraining unsafe or sensitive locations. |

## Where the utilities subsystem sits relative to its neighbors

Within `ts/packages/core`, these utilities act as the “shared substrate” for modules that coordinate sessions, tools, files, and providers. They are depended on by most of the core’s models and integration points—spanning routers, sessions, remote file mounts, and provider implementations—so utilities must stay small, deterministic, and type-safe.

Notably, the subsystem is also *a consumer* of the core’s error and type ecosystems. The utilities import error definitions and type contracts so that they can fail consistently and return values that match the rest of core’s expectations.

## Dependencies that shape utility design

The utilities subsystem deliberately leans on core’s shared types and error vocabulary rather than defining its own ad-hoc schemas. In the file dependency graph provided, the group depends on:

| Consumed module (imports) | Why it matters to utilities (as evidenced by imports) |
|---|---|
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/ComposioError.ts` and `ts/packages/core/src/errors/index.ts` | Utilities can surface failures in the same error language used across core. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/errors/FileModifierErrors.ts`, `PusherErrors.ts`, `SDKErrors.ts`, `SsrfErrors.ts`, `ToolErrors.ts`, `ValidationErrors.ts` | Utility behavior intersects with security- and tool-related failure modes, so error types stay centralized. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/telemetry/redact.ts` | Telemetry-safe handling/redaction is a cross-cutting utility concern that these helpers can apply. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/types/composio.types.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/types/customTool.types.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/types/files.types.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/types/tool.types.ts` | Utilities return typed data structures consistent with tool/file/session models. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/platform/node.ts` | Node-specific platform hooks are needed for runtime behaviors used by utilities (especially env/crypto/filesystem-adjacent helpers). |
| `ts/packages/core/src/provider/BaseProvider.ts` | Some utilities are provider-aware enough to support provider interactions. |
| `ts/packages/core/src/utils/modifiers/FileToolModifier.utils.neutral.ts` | File tool behavior is modified/normalized through utility-level modifiers. |
| `ts/packages/json-schema-to-zod/src/index.ts` | JSON schema handling integrates with Zod conversion, connecting the schema utilities to runtime validation tooling. |

## Serving the rest of core: how downstream modules use these utilities

Because many core models and routers are listed as consumers of this utility bundle, the subsystem functions less like a single “API” and more like a set of composable building blocks. Examples of downstream importers include:

- Router and session orchestration layers: `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterMcp.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/lib/toolRouterSessionDelete.ts`
- Domain models: `ts/packages/core/src/models/Files.node.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/models/RemoteFile.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/models/ToolRouterSessionFileMount.ts`, etc.
- Provider integration: `ts/packages/core/src/provider/OpenAIProvider.ts`

That downstream shape is consistent with the subsystem’s responsibilities: these utilities must handle low-level concerns (cancellation, schema conversion, MIME typing, response body parsing, sensitive path constraints) so routers and providers can focus on higher-level orchestration rather than re-implementing mechanics.

## Internal quality signals and operational risk profile

Recent git history shows the subsystem has a skew toward JSON/schema functionality:

- **Hotspots:** 3 files flagged as change hotspots, with `ts/packages/core/src/utils/jsonSchema.ts` being the most active (10 commits in 90 days).
- **Bus factor risk:** 15 files with a bus factor of one, meaning single-maintainer risk is present across a meaningful portion of the utility surface.
- **Potentially unused code:** several private symbols in this utilities group are not used anywhere (e.g., `MAX_REF_CHAIN_DEPTH`, `MAX_NODE_DEPTH`, `CYCLE_BREAK_SENTINEL`, and schema keyword collections like `SCHEMA_KEYWORDS`). This suggests either legacy/internal refactor leftovers or code paths intended for future use, which can affect maintainability and reviewer attention when changing schema logic.

There is also **hidden coupling** beyond the explicit dependency graph: this utilities set co-changes with `ts/packages/core` broadly and also with `python`, `ts/packages/cli`, and `ts/packages/json-schema-to-zod`, plus `ts/packages/providers/openai`. That coupling aligns with the utility functions’ cross-language and schema/tooling impact, particularly around JSON schema processing and tool argument/file handling.

## Why config defaults logic is excluded here

Although this utilities group includes env helpers (`ts/packages/core/src/utils/env.ts`) and constants (`ts/packages/core/src/utils/constants.ts`), the documentation scope explicitly excludes “config defaults logic.” That separation matters operationally: utilities here normalize inputs and enforce safe/consistent runtime behavior, while defaults and configuration policy are handled elsewhere, preventing policy decisions from being scattered across helper modules.

## What this subsystem is responsible for

This group is responsible for two closely related concerns:

1. **Default configuration materialization**
   - It defines default configuration object structure(s) and the types/fixtures that represent them (under `config-defaults`).
   - It includes a node-oriented default configuration entry (`ConfigDefaults.node.ts`) that downstream code can consume as “already shaped” config data.

2. **Transformation and modifier logic that converts tool/session/domain inputs into canonical core shapes**
   - Under `utils/transformers`, it normalizes response and context objects around tools, toolkits, authentication configs, connected accounts, usage, keyrings, and custom toolkits.
   - Under `utils/modifiers`, it provides modifier implementations (including file-related tool modifiers) that translate between file/tool concepts and core modifier/config types.

The group is explicitly shaped to be reused across multiple core models (e.g., `AuthConfigs`, `ConnectedAccounts`, `ToolRouterSession`, `Keyring`, and others), which is reflected in the dependency and depended-by sets: the models import the transformation utilities and config-defaults, but the transformation utilities themselves avoid provider communication and runtime telemetry.

## Key files and how they cluster

|---|---|---|
| Default config definitions & typing | `ts/packages/core/src/utils/config-defaults/types.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/utils/config-defaults/ConfigDefaults.node.ts` | Provide typed default configuration object(s) and a node-specific default surface that other parts of core can reference. |
| File/tool modifier core (hotspot) | `ts/packages/core/src/utils/modifiers/FileToolModifier.utils.neutral.ts` (and co-located `FileToolModifier.node.ts` implied by history signal) | Implements neutral file/tool modification utilities and supports node variants used heavily in recent bug-fix activity. |
| Tool-router & tool response normalization | `ts/packages/core/src/utils/transformers/toolRouterResponseTransform.ts` | Converts tool-router responses into the canonical core representation expected by downstream models/tests. |

## How the subsystem interacts with the rest of core

### Inputs it consumes (by dependency edges)
Across the import list, the subsystem’s transformers/modifiers repeatedly bind to core domain type modules, including:
- auth and connection state: `ts/packages/core/src/types/authConfigs.types.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/types/connectedAccountAuthStates.types.ts`, `ts/packages/core/src/types/connectedAccounts.types.ts`

- provider base types are referenced as an allowed dependency boundary (`ts/packages/core/src/provider/BaseProvider.ts`), but the subsystem is not intended to handle actual provider communication/telemetry; it prepares/normalizes shapes for the rest of the pipeline.

This pattern shows the subsystem is treated as a reusable “shape canonicalization” layer for model persistence (and later serialization), not as a transient CLI-only utility.

## Architectural decisions and the “shape hygiene” mindset

### Sanitize public docstrings in connected accounts
A notable implementation/maintenance decision exists around connected accounts: **public docstrings/JSDoc are sanitized to remove internal references** (e.g., Hermes PR numbers, backend storage details) and to correct incorrect statements about user/project relationships. This is described as a deliberate sweep aligned with a PR diff to prevent documentation leaks.

This decision reinforces the broader subsystem character: even though it is a transformation/defaulting layer, it is also a developer-facing API boundary where documentation cleanliness matters—especially for pieces derived from or presented alongside connected-account/auth configuration.

## Health and coupling signals that shape how it evolves

The subsystem’s recent activity and risk profile explain why it’s organized around typed transformers and modifiers rather than ad-hoc logic:

- **Hotspot concentration:** `ts/packages/core/src/utils/modifiers/FileToolModifier.node.ts` has most recent activity, and recent history indicates 11 bug-fix commits, “most in” that area. That implies the file/tool modification path has edge cases where normalization correctness and platform-specific behavior must be continuously maintained.
- **Bus factor concerns:** 5 files have a bus factor of one (single-maintainer risk). This is consistent with the subsystem’s broad surface area (79/113 public symbols) and the fact that changes likely ripple into many downstream models/tests.
- **Hidden coupling via history:** despite dependency graphs not explicitly explaining it, this group is co-changing with `ts/packages/core` (66 co-changing files) and also with `python` (16), `ts/packages/cli` (2), and provider packages (openai/anthropic with 1 each). That suggests default/config/transform shapes are part of a cross-language or cross-package contract, even when the import graph doesn’t show a direct coupling.
- **Potentially unused code:** several symbols are reported as having no importers (e.g., `CONFIG_DEFAULTS`, `schemaHasFileDownloadable`, `FileToolModifier`, and multiple private transformer helpers). This can be a symptom of ongoing refactors: some transformation utilities may have been superseded by newer code paths or routed differently through other exports/tests.

The “depended on by” list includes targeted tests that map directly to this subsystem’s responsibilities:

Because the subsystem is focused on defaults and transformation shaping, it avoids owning:
- **Runtime telemetry and provider communication** (explicitly excluded by scope).
- **Persistence mechanics** beyond providing canonical objects that `models/*` can store (the models are the persistence boundary consumers).
- **Validation logic re-implementation**: it uses shared schema/json-schema utilities and error types (`jsonSchema.ts`, `ValidationErrors.ts`, and friends) rather than inventing bespoke validation flows.

## What this providers package actually owns (and what it doesn’t)

This subsystem owns the provider entry points and the “glue” that makes an Anthropic-capable provider usable by the rest of the codebase: package-level `src/index.ts` exports, plus the shared typing/error surface seen in the Typesafe integration family (which is part of the Providers umbrella you navigate from here). Those exports are what downstream code imports (examples and e2e tests), while the detailed request/response semantics, provider-specific keys/policy rules, and any schema shaping are intentionally documented on the child concept pages.

It explicitly does **not** try to be the orchestration layer for the whole tool-routing system; the e2e tests and examples import into runtime/routers, while the provider implementations remain confined to the provider package boundary.

## How the package boundary fits with its neighbors

The Anthropic providers in `ts/packages/providers/anthropic` sit in the same provider architecture as other providers in this repo: they extend shared base provider classes in `ts/packages/core`, and they are consumed by e2e test runtimes and examples rather than being executed directly.

The cross-package relationship is visible in the class hierarchy spanning sibling providers: `VercelProvider`, `TypesafeProvider`, `MastraProvider`, `OpenAIAgentsProvider`, and `OpenAIResponsesProvider` all extend the shared base classes in `ts/packages/core/src/provider/BaseProvider.ts`. The concrete Anthropic provider entry points exposed from `ts/packages/providers/anthropic/src/index.ts` follow the same integration pattern—exposing a provider that can be mounted by higher-level routing/tooling code.

At a practical level, the subsystem is also coupled to build/release tooling via `tsdown.config.base.ts` and to shared UI/runtime utilities via the listed dependency `docs/components/terminal-kit/session/message.tsx` (indicating that provider testing or demo output likely interacts with terminal/session messaging).

## Vendor-adapter providers for Anthropic-adjacent families

Across the package set, the subsystem’s core concern is implementing provider classes that extend Mastra’s shared provider base types—so downstream code can treat different vendors uniformly. The class hierarchy makes this intent explicit: non-agentic vendors extend `BaseNonAgenticProvider`, while agentic vendors extend `BaseAgenticProvider`.

| Provider class | Base type it extends (from `ts/packages/core/src/provider/BaseProvider.ts`) | What that signals in practice |
|---|---|---|
| `AnthropicProvider` | `BaseNonAgenticProvider` | This adapter is used when the system expects a non-agentic provider contract (no agent orchestration responsibilities in this layer). |
| `OpenAIResponsesProvider` | `BaseNonAgenticProvider` | Included here to show how the same subsystem pattern is applied across vendor families (but this page focuses on the Anthropic provider family scope). |
| `GoogleProvider` | `BaseNonAgenticProvider` | Same adapter pattern for another non-agentic vendor. |
| `LangchainProvider` | `BaseAgenticProvider` | Uses the agentic provider contract variant. |
| `ClaudeAgentSDKProvider` | `BaseAgenticProvider` | Claude/agent SDK integration follows the agentic contract path. |
| `OpenAIAgentsProvider` | `BaseAgenticProvider` | Another agentic contract implementation that lives alongside these packages. |
| `LlamaindexProvider` | `BaseAgenticProvider` | Another agentic contract implementation. |
| `CloudflareProvider` | `BaseNonAgenticProvider` | Non-agentic variant of the same overall adapter concept. |
| `MastraProvider` | `BaseAgenticProvider` | Another agentic variant. |

That contract-first design is the reason the subsystem has a large footprint of exports and entrypoints: the provider implementations must be discoverable by code that constructs providers dynamically (in examples and in runtime/e2e harnesses).

## Entrypoints and cross-package wiring (what is exported, and where it starts)

The group’s public surface is mostly routed through `src/index.ts` entrypoints—each provider subpackage exposes an index that downstream code can import. The subsystem’s “shape” is therefore less about one monolithic implementation file and more about consistent wiring between entrypoints and provider classes, including schemas and adapter helpers.

|---|---|---|

Two additional provider-specific files stand out as “integration logic hubs” rather than pure re-exports:

- `ts/packages/providers/openai/src/OpenAIResponsesProvider.ts` (not Anthropic, but it’s the most active file in recent history, and it represents how the subsystem implements vendor-specific behavior behind the base-provider contract).
- `ts/packages/providers/mastra/src/relax-output-schema.ts` (a schema-oriented helper that reflects that providers often need to normalize/relax structured outputs to fit shared expectations).

## How this subsystem is used: examples and runtime tests

Downstream consumers in this repo import these provider packages in multiple contexts—showing that the subsystem must be stable across both interactive example code and automated runtime verification.

Key consumers include:

- Anthropic examples:
  - `ts/examples/anthropic/src/index.ts`
  - `ts/examples/anthropic/src/claude-agents-sdk.ts`
  - `ts/examples/anthropic/src/experimental.mcp.ts`

This usage pattern explains why the subsystem also depends on core and small UI/runtime support modules rather than being fully self-contained: it must produce values compatible with the rest of the system’s message and provider abstractions.

## Dependencies boundary: what it imports and what it intentionally does not own

The subsystem’s import edges are relatively controlled. It depends on the core contracts via `ts/packages/core/src/index.ts`, and it also relies on a terminal/message representation from `docs/components/terminal-kit/session/message.tsx`. That combination implies a pragmatic boundary:

- The provider implementations speak the shared “provider contract” defined by core.

pages.content:
## What this subsystem actually does: compile → classify → decide → respond

The Typesafe provider group is centered on turning inputs into provider-ready structures, then using a rules/criteria path to choose what to do next, and finally producing a standardized response object. The separation is visible across the core internal modules that are grouped under `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/`:

| Concern | Key file(s) | Observable subsystem responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Shared types and error model | `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/types.ts` | Defines `TypesafeProviderError` subclasses (including abstention and confirmation-required flows) and shapes the result types used downstream. |
| Compilation of inputs | `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/compile.ts` | Builds the compiled representation expected by later stages; it is directly covered by `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/test/compile.test.ts`. |
| Classification logic | `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/classify.ts` | Assigns inputs/requests to categories that influence the decision stage; covered by `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/test/classify.test.ts`. |
| Decision-making | `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/decide.ts` | Implements the next-step decision logic driven by the classified inputs; covered by `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/test/decide.test.ts` and also invoked indirectly in other tests. |
| Companion/assistance logic | `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/companion.ts` | Adds the “companion” behavior used by the integration path; it is also the most active file in recent history. |
| Response and validated output | `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/response.ts` | Produces response structures built around `AskResult` and `ValidatedAnswers`, and encodes “confirmation required / abstained” modes using the error hierarchy. |
| Keying/identifiers | `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/keys.ts` | Centralizes key constants or key derivation used by the above stages; it also exists alongside the compile/classify/decide pipeline. |
| Provider surface | `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/index.ts` | Exposes the provider implementation that other packages import (including examples and e2e runtimes). |
| Typesafe entry wiring | `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/tsdown.config.ts` | Controls the build/packaging for this provider family via `tsdown` configuration rather than runtime behavior. |

That pipeline is not just conceptual: the test suite spans each of the named stages (`classify`, `companion`, `compile`, `decide`, `execute`, `transport`, `live`), which indicates the subsystem is intended to be exercised end-to-end through the provider surface rather than only as isolated utilities.

## Boundaries and neighbors: what it consumes and what it deliberately leaves out

The Typesafe provider is implemented as a code-level integration for compilation/classification/decision and typed responses; it does not provide CLI functionality. This is consistent with two signals in the repository-level material:

- The dependency list includes CLI tooling packages (`@arethetypeswrong/cli`, `@changesets/cli`, `@changesets/read`), but those are external development tooling rather than runtime command implementations—matching the stated scope.
- The import edges show many consumers are examples and test harnesses (e.g. `ts/examples/typesafe/src/index.ts`, `ts/examples/vercel/src/ai.ts`, and multiple e2e/runtime entries), which is the expected usage pattern for a provider integration.

On the architectural side, the subsystem sits next to the core provider base types:

- It depends on `ts/packages/core/src/index.ts` (which is where the provider base classes live).
- It also relies on `tsdown.config.base.ts` for build-time configuration.

As a result, this subsystem’s persistence/transport boundaries are not implemented here in a CLI sense; instead, it delegates provider base behavior to core and focuses on its own typed interaction lifecycle.

## The provider-facing shape: typed errors and abstention/confirmation flows

A key design detail is the explicit error/decision taxonomy in `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/types.ts`. The class hierarchy includes multiple `TypesafeProviderError` subclasses, including at least:

- `TypesafeAbstainedDecisionError` (abstention behavior in the decision flow)
- `TypesafeApiError` (API-level failures)
- `TypesafeConfirmationRequiredError` (a “you must confirm” mode)

This matters because the rest of the subsystem (especially `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/decide.ts` and `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/response.ts`) needs to represent “can’t/shouldn’t act” and “needs confirmation” as first-class outcomes, not as generic thrown exceptions. That design is reinforced by the named tests: `companion.test.ts`, `decide.test.ts`, and `execute.test.ts` indicate the project expects these branches to be observable and stable.

`ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/response.ts` also establishes the response contract via `AskResult` extending `ValidatedAnswers`. That extension is the bridge between “decision logic” and “what consumers can safely read,” so downstream packages can treat classification/decision results as validated structured answers instead of ad-hoc payloads.

## Key integration points across packages (where it shows up)

This provider family is imported by both example apps and runtime/test harnesses, which implies it must be stable under real transport conditions (not only static compilation). The dependency list of “depended on by” includes:

- Cloudflare worker runtime router code: `ts/e2e-tests/runtimes/cloudflare/cf-workers-tool-router-ai/src/index.ts`
- TypeSafe examples: `ts/examples/typesafe/src/index.ts` and `ts/examples/typesafe/src/shortlist.ts`
- Tool-router and modifiers examples (which commonly exercise provider switching/loop behaviors): `ts/examples/tool-router/src/index.ts`, `ts/examples/tool-router/src/multi-account.ts`, and `ts/examples/modifiers/src/index.ts`
- Vercel examples that likely contrast provider implementations: `ts/examples/vercel/src/ai.ts`, `ts/examples/vercel/src/stream.ts`, `ts/examples/vercel/src/tool-loop-agent.ts`, `ts/examples/vercel/src/tool-router-ai.ts`
- Provider-specific tests, including `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/test/*` and Vercel tests in `ts/packages/providers/vercel/test/*`

Within this ecosystem, `ts/packages/providers/vercel/src/index.ts` functions as the Vercel provider surface (it is directly listed among the key files), while `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/index.ts` functions as the Typesafe provider surface for its own contract and staged logic.

## Operational character: hotspots, single-maintainer risk, and fix-heavy Vercel changes

The subsystem’s evolution signals a few pragmatic realities:

- 5 files flagged as change hotspots across the group (not limited to one file), and 7 files with bus factor one indicates that several integration-critical pieces are maintained by a single person.
- Recent bug-fix activity is concentrated in `ts/packages/providers/vercel/src/index.ts` (13 bug-fix commits), which suggests that while Typesafe provides the structured compile/classify/decide pipeline, the Vercel integration surface is where transport/provider edge cases were actively corrected.
- `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/companion.ts` is the most active file in recent history (4 commits in 90 days), aligning with the idea that the companion behavior is frequently tuned—likely because it affects downstream agent/tool flows.

## Key files (and how they relate to each other)

| File | Role within the subsystem | Neighbor relationship |
|---|---|---|
| `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/types.ts` | Defines the shared types and error hierarchy for the Typesafe provider flow | Consumed by decision/response logic and surfaced via provider APIs |
| `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/compile.ts` | Compiles inputs into the internal representation used later | Feeds classification/decision stages |
| `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/classify.ts` | Classifies requests/inputs to drive decisions | Feeds `decide.ts` |
| `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/decide.ts` | Determines the next action or abstention/confirmation outcome | Produces outcomes represented by Typesafe errors and response types |
| `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/companion.ts` | Implements companion logic used by the integration path | Most actively changed in recent history; likely influences execution behavior |
| `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/response.ts` | Builds `AskResult` / validated answers responses | Converts internal decisions into consumer-readable results |
| `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/src/keys.ts` | Centralizes identifiers/keys used by the pipeline | Supports consistent classification/compilation decisions |

| `ts/packages/providers/vercel/src/index.ts` | Provides the Vercel provider entry point used by Vercel examples/tests | Illustrates the sibling provider surface within the same “providers” family |
| `ts/packages/providers/typesafe/tsdown.config.ts` | Packaging/build configuration for this provider family | Ensures the subsystem is built/distributed correctly (build-time only) |

## Where the subsystem plugs into the build/test toolchain (without becoming a CLI)

Even though this subsystem is not responsible for CLI commands, the overall repository uses development tooling and build tooling that can affect provider behavior indirectly. For example, `tsdown` and the `tsdown.config.ts` file indicate that packaging is handled via `tsdown` rather than custom scripts. Similarly, the presence of test files for transport and live execution suggests the provider must integrate cleanly with transport adapters provided elsewhere in the codebase, while keeping the provider logic itself focused on compilation/classification/decision/response.

## Questions this page answers
- How does `ts/packages/providers/typesafe` structure the interaction lifecycle from compilation through classification and decision to the final response?

- Which files implement the “companion” behavior, and why is that behavior treated as integration-critical (based on recent activity and test coverage)?

pages.content:
## What this subsystem is responsible for (and what it is not)

Across `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/core/*` and `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/stores/*`, the package focuses on:

- Selecting an appropriate `CredentialStore` implementation for the current platform (Linux “secret tool”, macOS “security” via subprocess or FFI, or an unsupported fallback).
- Executing credential persistence operations through a persistence boundary that is shared across stores.
- Standardizing failure modes with `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/core/errors.ts`.
- Integrating with the project’s Effect v4 conventions via `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/effect.ts`.

What it deliberately leaves to other pages/modules: the “command orchestration” layer that decides *when* keys must be stored/read and *why* in the product workflow. That behavior is evidenced by imports from other parts of the CLI, but this package’s scope stays focused on storage mechanics rather than user-facing command sequencing.

## Credential store backends as the persistence boundary

The subsystem’s core design is a `CredentialStore` interface implemented by platform-specific stores in `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/core/store.ts`, with selection logic and shared helpers living near `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/stores/*` and `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/stores/shared.ts`.

The implementations cover:

- **Linux**: a tool-driven store in `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/stores/linux-secret-tool.ts`.
- **macOS**: two different backends—a subprocess-driven store and an FFI-driven store (`ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/stores/macos-security-subprocess.ts` and `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/stores/macos-security-ffi.ts`).
- **Fallback**: a store for unsupported platforms (`UnsupportedPlatformStore`) plus an in-memory implementation (`MemoryStore`) used as part of the bounded interface.
  
This split matters because the storage subsystem has to isolate the external mechanism differences while presenting a uniform capability to the rest of the CLI codebase.

## Effect v4 integration: shaping the execution model

The subsystem is explicitly built around the project’s Effect v4 migration. The file `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/effect.ts` is the integration point for the package’s effectful execution model, aligning the storage operations (including persistence and backend calls) with the repository’s Effect conventions.

This is not accidental layering; it is one of the key architectural decisions reflected in history: **“Migrate CLI refactor to Effect v4 (4.0.0-rc.112)”**. That decision drives how this package sequences potentially failing I/O while remaining consistent with the rest of the system that uses Effect v4 utilities.

## Persistence and errors: a consistent failure surface

The package keeps two concerns close to the core:

- **Persistence boundary**: `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/core/persistence.ts` provides the shared persistence mechanics used across store backends.
- **Error normalization**: `ts/packages/cli-keyring/src/core/errors.ts` centralizes the failure modes so the rest of the CLI does not need to understand backend-specific failure shapes.

The presence of dedicated tests (e.g., `test/errors.test.ts`, `test/ffi.test.ts`, `test/shared.test.ts`, and `test/entry.test.ts`) further indicates that the storage subsystem treats error and boundary behavior as first-class outputs, not just incidental implementation details.

pages.title: CLI Overview
pages.content:
## Where this subsystem fits in the CLI execution pipeline

Architecturally, `ts/packages/cli` is the orchestration layer for the command-line experience: it defines constants and UI primitives, loads and interprets configuration, gathers user context, and coordinates external service calls needed for tool execution and linking. The subsystem’s wiring is reinforced by its dependencies: it pulls in shared platform primitives from `ts/packages/core`, terminal/input UX from `docs/components/terminal-kit/input/input.tsx`, and authentication/key material behavior from `ts/packages/cli-keyring`.

The CLI’s behavior is shaped by two notable evolutions recorded in the repo history:

- **Tool execution and toolkit metadata moved to session-based Tool Router APIs**, replacing previous flag-driven configuration requirements for connected accounts. The CLI now routes certain command areas through session execution (`session.execute/executeMeta`) and supports a dual legacy/Tool Router v2 code path for connected-accounts linking, including actionable handling for `ToolRouterV2_NoActiveConnection`.
- **CLI help/command hierarchy was reorganized** by introducing a `composio manage` namespace for advanced resource management, routing existing aliases/help parsing through the new `manage` prefix to declutter top-level command UX.

These decisions are visible in how this subsystem exposes services and utilities (configuration, user context, composio client interaction, and terminal UI services) that downstream command implementations rely on—without this overview page re-describing each command.

## The core responsibilities: UX, configuration, user context, and Tool Router integration

`ts/packages/cli` concentrates responsibilities that are cross-cutting across many commands, rather than binding itself to a single command’s semantics:

- **Terminal UI and interaction**: the subsystem includes a terminal UI service (`ts/packages/cli/src/services/terminal-ui.ts`) and UI presentation helpers (e.g., colors in `ts/packages/cli/src/ui/colors.ts`), which allow commands to produce consistent interactive output.
- **Configuration and app-level effects**: configuration is centralized in `ts/packages/cli/src/services/config.ts`, while app configuration behavior is handled via effects (`ts/packages/cli/src/effects/app-config.ts`), keeping command code from duplicating configuration loading logic.
- **User context and runtime environment**: user-identity and execution context are modeled via `ts/packages/cli/src/services/user-context.ts`, complemented by host/environment inspection concerns represented in the class hierarchy around `HostEnvMarkers`/`RawHostEnvironment`.
- **Tool Router / composio client interactions**: integration with Composio-side services is represented by `ts/packages/cli/src/services/composio-clients.ts`, plus a key operational constant set (`ts/packages/cli/src/constants.ts`).
- **Schema transformation utilities used by integrations**: model utilities include JSON schema transformation (`ts/packages/cli/src/models/utils/json-transform-schema.ts`) and language/tooling builders are present as dependencies (`ts/packages/ts-builders`), supporting consistent typing/shape transformation across tool definitions.

The net effect is that commands can remain focused on “what” they do (toolkit actions, auth/config operations, etc.), while `ts/packages/cli` provides “how” they behave at runtime: consistent UX, configuration, and the integration plumbing required for tool execution.

## How the internal parts fit together (without command-by-command detail)

Even without enumerating each command, the subsystem’s structure makes a consistent flow clear:

1. **Constants and configuration establish runtime behavior**  
   `ts/packages/cli/src/constants.ts` and `ts/packages/cli/src/services/config.ts` provide shared values and configuration loading. App configuration effects in `ts/packages/cli/src/effects/app-config.ts` apply this setup in a way that commands can treat as a dependable runtime baseline.

2. **Interactive terminal UI mediates user-facing I/O**  
   `ts/packages/cli/src/services/terminal-ui.ts` and `ts/packages/cli/src/ui/colors.ts` standardize how CLI interactions are presented. This is consistent with the external dependency on `docs/components/terminal-kit/input/input.tsx`, which suggests the CLI UX is expected to be built from shared terminal kit primitives.

3. **User context and environment inspection inform auth and routing**  
   `ts/packages/cli/src/services/user-context.ts` provides the per-run context that other layers use (and is supported by the host/environment inspection classes listed in the class hierarchy). This matters because Tool Router session execution and connected-account linking require the CLI to know what “active” connection state is available at runtime.

4. **Tool execution is routed through Tool Router sessions (and handled gracefully on errors)**  
   `ts/packages/cli/src/services/composio-clients.ts` plus the architectural decision to use `session.execute/executeMeta` indicates the CLI’s tool execution path is session-first. The subsystem is also responsible for the dual legacy/v2 handling mentioned in the history, including actionable tips when there is no active Tool Router v2 connection.

5. **Model/schema utilities keep tool definitions and payloads coherent**  
   Utilities like `ts/packages/cli/src/models/utils/json-transform-schema.ts` ensure that tool-related schemas are transformed into the forms needed by the CLI’s typed model layer.

In practice, these pieces are designed to be reused across many commands, which aligns with the subsystem’s measurable risk profile in git history (large change hotspots and high bus factor concentration—discussed below).

The subsystem also contains a “skills sources” area (`ts/packages/cli/skills-src/composio-cli` and `ts/packages/cli/skills-src/composio-cli/references`), which indicates the CLI relies on curated references for building or mapping skills/tool definitions—those are part of this package’s integrated concern, even though the detailed behavior is better explained on the child pages.

## Build/release automation and CLI surface area live in child pages

This page intentionally does not re-document build scripts or the command surface. Instead, it points readers at the right places:

- `ts/packages/cli/scripts` — covers release and build automation tasks (what happens when building/publishing/upgrading).
- `ts/packages/cli/src` — covers the CLI runtime implementation in detail (how the entrypoints, command routing, and core orchestration are structured).

## Decisions that materially shape the codebase (as captured in history)

The CLI subsystem’s current shape is largely explained by the following coupled changes:

1. **Tool Router session-based execution**  
   The CLI introduced session-based execution for tool execution, toolkit list/info, and connected-accounts linking; it adds a helper (`createToolRouterSession`), rewrites the `ToolsExecutor` to use `session.execute/executeMeta`, and removes flags like `--connected-account-id` and `--toolkit-version`. It also maintains a legacy vs Tool Router v2 dual code path for connected-accounts linking and explicitly handles `ToolRouterV2_NoActiveConnection` with actionable tips, with test/mocks updated for `TestLiveInput.toolRouter`.

2. **Command hierarchy cleanup via `composio manage` namespace**  
   The CLI introduced a `composio manage` namespace for advanced commands and routes existing aliases/help parsing through a new `manage` prefix to declutter top-level CLI help.

3. **User-visible upgrade download behavior and archive payload reduction**  
   The CLI upgrade download path was adjusted to provide feedback and to reduce wasted payload bytes. The history notes that a prior implementation had only an invisible debug log signal because the body was read with a single buffered `response.arrayBuffer`, and also that a large archive portion was unpacking binaries for platforms the host cannot execute.

4. **Version authority moved to GitHub releases for CLI binaries**  
   Standalone binaries now treat GitHub release tag versions as the authority, replacing private package semver with a `0.0.0-development` sentinel and injecting/verifying the exact release tag version during build. Regression coverage was added, and changesets were avoided for CLI packages.

Separately, repo-wide toolchain migrations also impact this subsystem’s maintenance patterns:
- **Migrate eslint to oxlint and typecheck to TypeScript 7**, including adding a TS6 pin for JS compiler API consumers and removing sibling-src path mappings to avoid accidental `.d.ts` emission during dependent package builds.

## Operational characteristics: maintainability pressure and change coupling

This subsystem shows strong “central wiring” behavior typical of orchestration code:

- **High churn areas**: 72 files flagged as change hotspots and **351 bug-fix commits** in recent history, with a large fraction tied to `ts/packages/cli/src/commands/setup.cmd.ts`.
- **Single-maintainer risk**: 89 files have a bus factor of one. That aligns with the fact that orchestration/UX/config glue tends to be concentrated in fewer developers.
- **Hidden coupling with the builder and CLI e2e suites**: co-changing history includes `ts/packages/ts-builders` and specific e2e tests (`ts/e2e-tests/cli/toolkits/list`, `ts/e2e-tests/cli/toolkits/search`), plus a small shared “test” surface co-changing.

These signals are consistent with the subsystem being a boundary layer: it changes when either the underlying integrations (Tool Router, composio clients, schemas) or the user-facing CLI contract (help structure, connected-account linking behavior, upgrade UX) change.

- `ts/packages/cli/scripts` — for release/build automation specifics and upgrade/release behaviors.
- `ts/packages/cli/src` — for the actual CLI runtime implementation: entrypoints, routing, and how command execution ties back to the services described above.
